purpose: Additional source-backed retrieval and exam prompts for DSA5208.

questions.prompt: Why is reporting only average runtime weak evidence for a distributed-system claim?
questions.solution: An average hides worker count, partitioning, communication, coordination, skew, and failure behavior. Those conditions must be recorded to make the claim reproducible.
questions.explanation: Distributed performance is a systems measurement problem, not only an algorithm-complexity number.
questions.misconception: One runtime number is not a complete experiment.

questions.prompt: State the message-passing assumptions used by Lecture 1.
accepted: no shared global memory and message passing
questions.solution: Processes do not share a common global memory and communicate solely by passing messages.
questions.explanation: The model defines what a process can know directly.
questions.misconception: Do not add a shared-memory assumption.

questions.prompt: What is H in the lecture notation?
choices: The union of all process event histories
questions.explanation: H is the union of the local event histories.
questions.misconception: Events and processes are different objects.
questions.visualHook: Trace the local histories into the global event set.

questions.prompt: State the three rules that generate happens-before.
accepted: local order send before receive transitivity
same process order message order transitive closure
questions.solution: Use local process order, send-before-receive, and transitivity.
questions.explanation: These rules define causal precedence without a global clock.
questions.misconception: Wall-clock order is not one of the generating rules.

questions.prompt: What must be true before two events can be called concurrent?
questions.solution: Neither event happens-before the other; both directions fail under the causal relation.
questions.explanation: Concurrency is a positive incomparability condition.
questions.misconception: Failure to prove one direction is not enough.
questions.visualHook: Compare both directions in the causal graph.

questions.prompt: Which guarantee preserves message order on one channel?
questions.explanation: FIFO preserves send order for messages on the same channel.
questions.misconception: FIFO is weaker than system-wide causal ordering.

questions.prompt: Why can causal ordering require a receiver buffer?
accepted: earlier message may not arrive yet
questions.solution: The receiver may receive a later message before a causally earlier one, so it buffers the later message until the dependency arrives.
questions.explanation: Stronger delivery guarantees require state and waiting.
questions.misconception: The receiver cannot deliver every arrival immediately under causal ordering.

questions.prompt: Given $T_1=10$, $T_2=14$, $T_3=20$, and $T_4=28$, compute the NTP round-trip delay estimate.
questions.explanation: The formula compares client-side and server-side elapsed intervals.
questions.misconception: Do not add all four timestamps.

questions.prompt: Why does NTP not prove that one event caused another?
accepted: physical time is not causal order
questions.solution: NTP estimates physical time under delay assumptions; causality is defined by event and message relations.
questions.explanation: Synchronization and causal ordering answer different questions.
questions.misconception: A synchronized wall clock is not a causal oracle.
questions.visualHook: Compare physical and logical time layers.

questions.prompt: A local scalar clock is 4 and a received message carries 7. What is the receive timestamp when $d=1$?
questions.explanation: The receive event must be after both known histories.

questions.prompt: Why can scalar timestamps order concurrent events?
accepted: scalar clocks are not strongly consistent
concurrent events may have ordered values
questions.solution: Scalar clocks preserve causal order in one direction but do not prove causality from timestamp order.
questions.explanation: The artificial total order can be useful while still being incomplete for concurrency detection.
questions.misconception: An increasing scalar value does not imply happens-before.
questions.visualHook: Compare scalar and vector clock limits.

questions.prompt: Compare $X=(2,1)$ and $Y=(1,2)$. What is the relation?
questions.solution: They are concurrent because $X$ is larger in the first component while $Y$ is larger in the second.
questions.explanation: Neither vector is componentwise below the other.

questions.prompt: What is the message-size trade-off of a basic vector clock?
questions.solution: A vector contains one component per process, so each message carries $O(n)$ timestamp metadata.
questions.explanation: Vector clocks recover more causal information at a larger communication cost.
questions.misconception: Vector clocks are not constant-size metadata.
questions.visualHook: Scale the number of process components.

questions.prompt: Why can a sender omit unchanged vector entries for one receiver?
questions.solution: The receiver has already observed the prior values from the last message on that sender-receiver pair, so only changed entries need to be sent.
questions.misconception: Compression may omit repetition, not required causal knowledge.

questions.prompt: Which technique reduces the timestamp storage order from quadratic to linear in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The differential technique maintains Last Sent and Last Update vectors.
questions.misconception: Vector compression and scalar clocks solve different problems.
questions.visualHook: Compare recent-vector storage with LS/LU state.

questions.prompt: Which model additionally preserves real-time order between non-overlapping operations?
questions.explanation: Linearizability preserves a legal sequence and also respects real-time non-overlap; sequential consistency keeps one legal sequence without the same real-time constraint.
questions.misconception: One common sequence is not automatically the same as preserving real-time order.
questions.visualHook: Compare the strict and sequential consistency examples.

questions.prompt: Why are MongoDB read concern "majority" and write concern "majority" still not enough by themselves to guarantee read-your-writes consistency by definition?
accepted: majority snapshot can lag the client write
need session or lamport clock state
read may hit node not caught up to that client
questions.solution: A read served from a majority-committed snapshot can still miss the client's latest write on that serving node. MongoDB therefore adds session or Lamport-clock state so the read waits until the node has caught up to that client's write.
questions.explanation: Majority visibility and one client's session guarantee are related but not identical.
questions.misconception: A majority acknowledgement does not automatically guarantee that every possible reader already provides the client's session guarantee.
questions.visualHook: Inspect the majority snapshot and Lamport-clock enforcement slides together.

sourceRefs.role: MongoDB read-your-writes implementation with Lamport clocks
